headline: Missouri cannabis taxes near $1B on $6.24B in sales, trade group says
dek: MoCannTrade says Missouri cannabis sales had raised $992 million in state and local sales taxes by October 2026, with $265 million in the last 12 months.
key_points: The Missouri Cannabis Trade Association put cumulative cannabis sales tax revenue at $992.02 million through October 2026, on $6.24 billion of sales since October 2020.
The state has received $609.19 million and local governments $382.82 million, according to the group's analysis reported by KCTV5.
The last 12 months produced $265.47 million, which on our arithmetic is about $22 million a month, enough to carry the total past $1 billion during November.
The figures come from an industry group and include ordinary sales tax as well as cannabis-specific taxes; they exclude licence fees and payroll taxes.
body: Missouri's legal cannabis market has all but reached $1 billion in sales tax paid to state and local governments, six years after the first medical sale. The Missouri Cannabis Trade Association, known as MoCannTrade, said this week that cumulative cannabis sales tax revenue stood at $992.02 million through October 2026, according to a report by KCTV5 in Kansas City on Thursday 19 November.

The group described the total as having passed $1 billion. Its own figures to the end of October stop just short. The last 12 months brought in $265.47 million, which is about $22.1 million a month on our arithmetic. At that pace the remaining $8 million would have been collected within the first two weeks of November. The milestone is real or within days of it; the exact date is a matter of which month's data is counted.
## What the number includes

The total is broader than a cannabis excise figure. MoCannTrade says it includes regular state and local sales taxes charged on cannabis purchases as well as the voter-approved taxes that apply only to medical and adult-use marijuana, KCTV5 reports. It does not include licensing fees, payroll taxes or other economic contributions.

That matters for comparisons. As we reported on 20 November, Michigan collected $287.2 million from its adult-use excise tax alone in its 2025-26 fiscal year. Missouri's $265.47 million for the 12 months to October counts general sales tax too, so the two are not like for like. What the Missouri figure does show is the full sales-tax take from one product category.

Sales since the first legal medical purchase in October 2020 total $6.24 billion, the group says. Adult-use sales began in February 2023, Ganjapreneur notes. Dividing cumulative tax by cumulative sales gives an effective rate of about 15.9% over the life of the programme. That is our calculation, and it blends the medical years, when rates were lower, with the adult-use years.
## Who gets the money

The state has received $609.19 million of the total, or about 61%. Local governments where licensed dispensaries operate have received $382.82 million, about 39%. The local share is made up of the local portion of regular sales tax plus a 3% adult-use marijuana tax that applies in most areas, according to the group's analysis.
MoCannTrade listed where the state's share has gone, as reported by KCTV5:

$186.74 million to state general revenue. $132.77 million to veterans' healthcare through the Missouri Veterans Commission. $66.79 million to the state's Substance Use Disorder Grant Program. $66.79 million to the public defender system. $62.25 million to public education. $7.79 million to conservation. $6.23 million to the state parks and soils programme.

Those seven lines add up to $529.36 million. That leaves about $79.8 million of the state's $609.19 million not itemised in the list. The report does not say where that remainder sits; programme administration costs and funds not yet distributed are possible explanations, but we have not seen a breakdown.
> Missouri's cannabis tax take is running at about three times what voters were told to expect. The forecasts were wrong in the state's favour.
## Ahead of the forecasts

The group's sharpest claim is about expectations. It says the $265.47 million generated in the 12 months to October is roughly three times the combined annual estimates attached to the state's two ballot measures. Those estimates appeared in state auditor fiscal notes before the 2018 medical vote and the 2022 adult-use vote, according to MoCannTrade.

Andrew Mullins, the association's executive director, said in a statement that the state can expect "many billions" more in sales tax revenue in the decades ahead. That is a trade group's projection, not a state forecast.

The source deserves a note of caution. MoCannTrade represents licensed operators and has an interest in showing that the regulated market pays its way. The underlying sales data is published monthly by the state, and KCTV5 linked to it, but the tax totals and the allocation list in this story are the association's analysis. We have not checked them against state revenue records.
## Why it matters now

The figures arrive during a period of rule changes for Missouri's market. State regulators proposed new rule amendments this month. The state's law capping hemp-derived THC products took effect on 12 November, as we have reported, which pushes intoxicating products towards the licensed and taxed channel. And the Division of Cannabis Regulation has warned licensees that federal rescheduling does not permit interstate sales.

For operators, a tax take three times the forecast is a strong argument in any debate over licence caps, tax rates or local opt-outs. For local governments, $382.82 million over six years is a reason to keep dispensaries inside city limits. For other states weighing legalization, including several where bills are being filed for 2027, Missouri is a reference point for a mid-sized market: about $6.2 billion in sales and close to $1 billion in tax in six years, by the industry's count.
## What to watch

Watch the state's November sales data, which should confirm whether the cumulative total has passed $1 billion. Watch whether monthly tax receipts hold near $22 million through the winter. Watch the 2027 legislative session for proposals to change how cannabis revenue is divided. And watch whether the hemp THC law that took effect on 12 November shows up as higher dispensary sales in the months ahead.
